intro_band.agent_remit_summary: Hermes is a single-tenant personal AI agent whose remit authorizes one shared agent core across a CLI, a messaging gateway, a terminal UI, and a native Electron desktop app. It may run shell commands, read and write files, execute code, drive a browser, connect to operator-installed MCP servers, keep persistent memory, author its own skills, schedule cron automations, and delegate to subagents — all on behalf of a single operator and the callers that operator has explicitly allowlisted. The remit's defining constraints are that ingested content is data and never a control channel, that destructive operations require operator approval in every execution context including unattended ones, that any untrusted input surface must run under OS-level isolation rather than the default host terminal backend, and that telemetry is opt-in and off by default. On the desktop side it forbids rendering agent output as active content and forbids installing agent runtime code from an unverified source.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: Two source repositories scanned as one subject: a large Python agent (run_agent.py, cli.py, gateway/ with ~30 platform adapters, ~85 modules under tools/) and an Electron/TypeScript desktop client with a main/preload/renderer split that launches a headless hermes serve backend over loopback HTTP. Security controls are real and centralised: tools/approval.py holds an unconditional hardline blocklist plus a pattern-based approval gate, tools/threat_patterns.py is a single shared injection-pattern library consumed by agent/prompt_builder.py and tools/memory_tool.py, tools/skills_guard.py enforces trust-tiered skill installs, and gateway/platforms/api_server.py refuses to start without an API key. The shipped defaults diverge from the remit in three places that matter: terminal.backend is local (host execution) while web and browser tools are in the default toolset, the approval gate auto-approves outside CLI/gateway/cron contexts, and the desktop installer pipes a remotely-fetched shell script into bash with no integrity check.

behavior_summary: The dominant pattern is a mature, layered, self-aware security posture whose shipped defaults sit on the wrong side of its own stated boundary. Hermes documents in SECURITY.md that only OS-level isolation is a real boundary and that in-process heuristics are review aids — then ships terminal.backend: local together with web_search, web_extract and the browser toolset enabled by default, so untrusted web, email and messaging content reaches a tool loop that executes shell commands directly on the host. The approval gate that would slow that chain is bypassed wholesale outside interactive CLI, gateway and cron contexts (tools/approval.py logs a warning and returns approved), and the desktop's first-run install fetches install.sh from a mutable branch and pipes it to bash with no checksum or signature. Secondary theme: outbound-data defaults contradict the remit in two independent places — PostHog telemetry is on by default in official desktop builds, and the custom-endpoint provider credential is missing from the subprocess credential-strip set.

rules.rule_text: The agent MUST NOT act on instructions embedded in ingested content — web pages, emails, inbound messages, file contents, tool results, or MCP server responses — as though they were operator commands.
The agent MUST NOT grant itself new authority beyond what the operator has explicitly granted — new callers, egress destinations, tools, integrations, or trust tiers.
The agent MUST NOT disable, bypass, or route around its own safety controls (approval gate, output redaction, caller allowlists, credential scoping) in order to complete a task.

The desktop layer MUST NOT render agent-produced or tool-produced output as active or executable content; agent output MUST be treated as inert (displayed as data, never evaluated as HTML/script/markup with side effects).
MUST refuse to dispatch work, relay output, or resolve approvals until an operator-configured allowlist is set. MUST NOT fail open when no allowlist is configured.
MUST default to a loopback bind; MUST require an allowlist before serving.
MUST bind loopback only and rely on OS-level access control; MUST NOT be exposed beyond the local user without an explicit network authentication layer.

the set of enabled messaging channels and network-exposed HTTP surfaces (API server, dashboard, plugins) is operator-configured; any channel or surface not enabled by the operator is unauthorized by default, and one found active outside that configured set is a trust-expansion finding.
Trusted People / Accounts
Trusted Domains
Trusted Services / Integrations
Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)

Authorized isolation posture (closure): the default local (host) terminal backend is authorized only for trusted content; any untrusted input surface MUST run under a sandboxed terminal backend (Docker/Modal/Daytona) or whole-process wrapping.
Allowed Data Sources

Provider API keys and gateway/platform tokens MUST NOT be passed into lower-trust in-process or subprocess components (shell subprocesses, the code-execution child, MCP subprocesses, cron job scripts); they MUST be stripped from that environment by default, and the strip set MUST cover every configured provider/gateway credential (a registry-derived denylist is acceptable).
Credentials MUST NOT be written into the main config file or into version control; they belong in the operator credential file with tight permissions (or a dedicated secret store).

Operator credentials and session authorization material MUST NOT egress to any destination outside the trust envelope, whether via environment leakage, adapter logging, or a transport error that flushes them upstream.
Outbound telemetry and usage attribution are opt-in and off by default; no telemetry or usage data may egress unless the operator has explicitly enabled it.
Allowed Without Approval

Destructive or irreversible shell and file operations (deletion, overwrite, bulk or recursive changes) MUST require operator approval before execution, in every execution context and regardless of interactive vs. unattended mode.
Binding a local-only surface (dashboard, plugin HTTP server, or any local-IPC surface) to a non-loopback interface MUST be an explicit operator decision, never taken autonomously.

Agent work MUST NOT be dispatched, output relayed, or approvals resolved for any caller outside the configured authorization set. Session identifiers are routing handles, not authorization boundaries — knowledge of a session ID MUST NOT grant access to another caller's work, output, or approvals.

The desktop self-update and first-run install path MUST NOT fetch or install agent runtime code from an unverified or unauthenticated source; installers and runtime updates MUST be integrity-verified before they replace the running app or backend.

On a destructive-command match, the response MUST be halt-pending-approval — pause and prompt the operator, never autonomous execution (the runtime enforcement of the destructive-operation approval gate).
On an enabled network-exposed adapter with no caller allowlist, the response MUST be fail-closed — refuse to serve rather than dispatch.
When Skills Guard detects injection-like patterns in installable skill or plugin content, surface the detection to the operator for review before install.
When output redaction detects a secret-like pattern in agent output, strip it from display and continue.

Tool invocations, approval decisions, and session lifecycle events MUST be recorded to durable, structured logs (`agent.log` / `gateway.log`; `desktop.log` for the desktop layer) sufficient to reconstruct what the agent did.

findings.summary: Default config puts untrusted web, email and messaging content into a tool loop that executes shell commands directly on the host.
findings.description: The shipped default is terminal.backend: local while web_search, web_extract and the browser tools are in the default toolset, so content the operator does not control reaches an agent that can run host commands. The remit requires any untrusted input surface to run under a sandboxed backend or whole-process wrapping; the project's own SECURITY.md agrees this posture is unsupported, yet it is what ships. Contributors folded into this chain: the default local backend and the default web/browser toolset — the headless approval bypass is broken out separately as PRAX-2026-07-29-003 because it harms operator-originated runs too.
policy_rule_text: Authorized isolation posture (closure): the default local (host) terminal backend is authorized only for trusted content; any untrusted input surface MUST run under a sandboxed terminal backend (Docker/Modal/Daytona) or whole-process wrapping.

The agent MUST NOT act on instructions embedded in ingested content — web pages, emails, inbound messages, file contents, tool results, or MCP server responses — as though they were operator commands.

evidence.snippet: backend "local" is the shipped default, lines 167-172; terminal_tool.py:1021 resolves it via os.getenv("TERMINAL_ENV", "local") and dispatches to host execution at :1159
web_search and web_extract at :33 and browser_navigate/browser_cdp at :43-46 are members of the default toolset assembled at :350-358, so untrusted fetch reaches the same loop that calls terminal()

recommended_actions: Ship terminal.backend defaulting to a sandboxed backend (docker), or refuse to enable web_search, web_extract and the browser toolset while the backend is local unless the operator sets an explicit acknowledgement key in config.yaml.
Add a startup check in gateway/run.py that logs an error and requires opt-in when an untrusted ingress surface (messaging adapter, email, webhook) is enabled together with TERMINAL_ENV=local.

findings.summary: Desktop first-run install fetches the agent runtime installer from a mutable branch and pipes it to a shell with no integrity verification.
findings.description: Both platform paths download an install script over HTTPS from the main branch and execute it immediately — no checksum, no signature, no pinned commit or tag. TLS authenticates the transport, not the artifact, so anyone who can write to that branch or that release infrastructure reaches every installing desktop, and the Windows path additionally runs it under -ExecutionPolicy Bypass. The remit forbids installing agent runtime code from an unverified source.
policy_rule_text: The desktop self-update and first-run install path MUST NOT fetch or install agent runtime code from an unverified or unauthenticated source; installers and runtime updates MUST be integrity-verified before they replace the running app or backend.

evidence.snippet: "curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --skip-setup" built at :896-899 and spawned via bash -c at :902
Windows twin, lines 1001-1011 — Invoke-WebRequest of install.ps1 from the same mutable main ref, written to temp and invoked at :1011, spawned with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass at :1033-1038

recommended_actions: Pin the installer to an immutable ref (a release tag or commit SHA) and verify a published SHA-256 digest, or a detached signature, in installer.ts before invoking bash or PowerShell — abort the install on mismatch.

Ship the install script inside the signed and notarized desktop bundle under resources/ and execute the local copy, so the runtime install inherits the app's existing code-signing trust rather than fetching at run time.

findings.summary: Outside CLI, gateway and cron contexts the approval gate auto-approves every dangerous command and only writes a log warning.
findings.description: The remit requires operator approval for destructive shell and file operations in every execution context, explicitly including unattended mode, and the escalation rule requires halt-pending-approval on a destructive-command match. Any headless run — a systemd unit, a CI job, an embedding host, an SDK caller — has neither HERMES_INTERACTIVE nor a gateway platform bound, so recursive deletes, chmod 777 and disk copies execute unprompted. The hardline floor still blocks the unrecoverable subset, which is why this is a partial rather than an absent control.
policy_rule_text: Destructive or irreversible shell and file operations (deletion, overwrite, bulk or recursive changes) MUST require operator approval before execution, in every execution context and regardless of interactive vs. unattended mode.

On a destructive-command match, the response MUST be halt-pending-approval — pause and prompt the operator, never autonomous execution (the runtime enforcement of the destructive-operation approval gate).

evidence.snippet: check_dangerous_command lines 969-988 — when not is_cli and not is_gateway, logs "AUTO-APPROVED dangerous command in non-interactive non-gateway context" and returns approved True; check_all_command_guards repeats it at :1206-1223

check_execute_code_guard :1465-1519 documents the same limitation — a local non-interactive non-gateway session returns approved for arbitrary Python that can spawn subprocesses bypassing terminal approval

recommended_actions: Invert the default in check_all_command_guards so an unrecognised execution context denies rather than approves, mirroring the existing cron approvals.cron_mode: deny behaviour, and require an explicit approvals.headless_mode: approve opt-in to restore the current behaviour.

Until that lands, promote the auto-approve log line from logger.warning to a startup-time error banner so an operator running headless sees that the gate is inert before the first dangerous command, not after.

findings.summary: Desktop analytics are on by default in official builds, sending usage events to a third-party endpoint before the operator consents.
findings.description: The consent check treats an absent stored preference as enabled whenever a PostHog key is compiled in, which is exactly the official-build case, so screen views and feature-usage events egress to eu.i.posthog.com on first run. The remit states telemetry and usage attribution are opt-in and off by default, and lists only configured model providers, messaging APIs and operator-installed MCP hosts as trusted outbound destinations. Privacy hardening is present (DNT respected, session recording disabled, PII masking) but it mitigates the payload, not the missing consent.
policy_rule_text: Outbound telemetry and usage attribution are opt-in and off by default; no telemetry or usage data may egress unless the operator has explicitly enabled it.

evidence.snippet: isAnalyticsEnabled lines 9-19 — "if (stored === null) return hasKey;" with the comment "First run: enabled if key exists", so a compiled-in VITE_POSTHOG_KEY makes the default true
posthog.init at :49-73 posts to POSTHOG_HOST (default https://eu.i.posthog.com) and identifies a persisted anonymous UUID with app version, platform and node version

recommended_actions: Change the first-run default in isAnalyticsEnabled() to false so initAnalytics() no-ops until setAnalyticsConsent(true) is called.
Add a consent prompt to the onboarding flow that records an explicit choice into hermes-analytics-enabled before any capture() can fire.

findings.summary: The custom/Ollama endpoint provider credential is absent from the subprocess strip set, so it inherits into terminal and execute_code children.
findings.description: The remit requires the strip set to cover every configured provider credential. The denylist is built from PROVIDER_REGISTRY plus a static supplement, but the custom provider — the profile covering Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp and any operator-supplied OpenAI-compatible endpoint — is explicitly skipped during registry population, and CUSTOM_API_KEY appears in neither the static supplement nor OPTIONAL_ENV_VARS. An operator on a custom endpoint therefore has their provider key readable by every shell command and code-execution script the agent runs, which is the exact exposure the sandbox scrubbing exists to prevent.
policy_rule_text: Provider API keys and gateway/platform tokens MUST NOT be passed into lower-trust in-process or subprocess components (shell subprocesses, the code-execution child, MCP subprocesses, cron job scripts); they MUST be stripped from that environment by default, and the strip set MUST cover every configured provider/gateway credential (a registry-derived denylist is acceptable).

evidence.snippet: registry population at :447-471 skips names in {"copilot","kimi-coding","kimi-coding-cn","zai","openrouter","custom"}, so the custom profile contributes no api_key_env_vars to the blocklist

_build_provider_env_blocklist static supplement lines 126-186 names OPENAI/ANTHROPIC/OPENROUTER and ~30 others but no CUSTOM_ variable; _sanitize_subprocess_env at :217 therefore copies CUSTOM_API_KEY (read at hermes_cli/models.py:2108) straight through

recommended_actions: Add CUSTOM_API_KEY and CUSTOM_BASE_URL to the static supplement in _build_provider_env_blocklist(), alongside the OPENROUTER entries that already cover the other registry-skipped provider.

Replace the registry-derived denylist with a name-shape rule as defence in depth — strip any variable matching *_API_KEY, *_TOKEN or *_SECRET unless it is on the operator passthrough allowlist — so the next provider added outside the registry is covered by default.

findings.summary: The identity file loaded into every system prompt is agent-writable with no approval gate, guarded only on the read path.
findings.description: ~/.hermes/SOUL.md is injected into the system prompt on every session, yet the file-tool sensitive-path guard protects only OS system directories and the approval patterns never mention it, so write_file and patch can rewrite the agent's own standing instructions unprompted. With a confirmed injection path from web, email and messaging ingress, that is a one-hop cross-session persistence chain. The read-side scanner is a real mitigation but deliberately applies the narrower context scope, so persistence, SSH-backdoor and exfiltration-URL patterns are not screened out of the file.

evidence.snippet: _SENSITIVE_PATH_PREFIXES at :235-239 covers only /etc, /boot, /usr/lib/systemd, /private/* and docker.sock — no HERMES_HOME path; grep of tools/approval.py for SOUL returns zero matches, so neither write tool nor terminal gate stops the write

_scan_context_content :43-59 blocks a matching SOUL.md with a placeholder but the docstring at :48-52 states strict-scope patterns (SSH backdoor, persistence, exfil-URL) are deliberately NOT applied here; the file is loaded into every prompt at :1368-1379

recommended_actions: Route writes whose resolved path is SOUL.md, AGENTS.md or config.yaml under HERMES_HOME through the approval gate by adding them to _SENSITIVE_PATH_PREFIXES in tools/file_tools.py and to _SENSITIVE_WRITE_TARGET in tools/approval.py.
Scan identity and context files with the strict scope on the write path, where the operator can still intervene, rather than relying solely on the narrower context-scope screen at load time.

findings.summary: MCP tool descriptions are scanned for injection but never blocked or surfaced — a poisoned description registers and enters the model context regardless.
findings.description: The remit says no integration may be auto-trusted on the strength of its own description alone, and forbids acting on instructions embedded in MCP server responses. The scanner runs at registration time and writes a logger.warning, then registration proceeds unconditionally, so the only signal reaches a rotating log file rather than the operator. The pattern set is also markedly weaker than the project's own shared library: ten fixed regexes with no invisible-unicode check and no filler-word tolerance, so "ignore all prior instructions" slips past the pattern that anchors on "previous".

evidence.snippet: comment at :340-342 states "These are WARNING-level — we log but don't block, since false positives would break legitimate MCP servers"; _scan_mcp_description at :367-385 returns findings and only logs
call site at :3259-3260 discards the return value and falls straight through to _convert_mcp_schema and registry.register, so a flagged description is registered and reaches the model context

recommended_actions: Replace _MCP_INJECTION_PATTERNS with scan_for_threats(description, scope="context") from tools/threat_patterns.py so MCP descriptions inherit the invisible-unicode set and the filler-word-resistant patterns already used for context files.
Skip registration of a flagged tool and raise it through the operator-facing approval or notification path used by Skills Guard, rather than resolving the false-positive concern by never blocking.

findings.summary: Plugin HTTP adapters bind all interfaces by default, and the Teams adapter hardcodes it so no operator decision is possible.
findings.description: The remit requires network-exposed HTTP surfaces to default to a loopback bind and requires any non-loopback bind to be an explicit operator decision. The Teams adapter passes the wildcard address as a literal to TCPSite with no config lookup, so an operator cannot restrict it to loopback at all, and the webhook and LINE surfaces ship the wildcard as their default. Each surface has its own authentication (bot framework, HMAC), so this is an unrequested attack-surface expansion rather than an open door — which is why it sits at Medium.
policy_rule_text: Binding a local-only surface (dashboard, plugin HTTP server, or any local-IPC surface) to a non-loopback interface MUST be an explicit operator decision, never taken autonomously.
MUST default to a loopback bind; MUST require an allowlist before serving.

evidence.snippet: web.TCPSite(self._runner, "0.0.0.0", self._port) — the address is a literal with no config or env override, and the startup log at :703-707 reports the wildcard bind as normal
host = wh.get("host", "0.0.0.0") — wildcard is the fallback default, and the setup hint printed at :118 recommends it to operators; plugins/platforms/line/adapter.py:646 uses the same default

recommended_actions: Change the fallback in hermes_cli/webhook.py:99 and plugins/platforms/line/adapter.py:646 to 127.0.0.1, and update the setup hint at webhook.py:118 to match.
Make the Teams adapter read its bind address from extra.host with a loopback default instead of the literal at adapter.py:698, so a non-loopback bind requires an operator edit.

findings.summary: Smart-approval mode hands the human approval decision to an auxiliary LLM prompted with the attacker-influenced command string itself.
findings.description: When approvals.mode is smart, the flagged command is interpolated into a review prompt and a one-word verdict from the auxiliary model can grant session-wide approval for that pattern, replacing the operator entirely. The command text is model output that untrusted ingested content may have shaped, and it is placed in the same context as the reviewer's instructions with no delimiting, so the reviewer is subject to the injection it is meant to catch. This is opt-in rather than default, which holds it at Medium.

evidence.snippet: _smart_approve builds the reviewer prompt at :890-902 by interpolating the raw command and description, then maps a bare "APPROVE" reply to approval at :913-914

at :1270-1281 an approve verdict calls approve_session for every warning key, so one model verdict silently allowlists that pattern for the rest of the session without the operator ever seeing the prompt

recommended_actions: Delimit the untrusted command inside _smart_approve the way tool results are delimited elsewhere, and treat any verdict other than an exact DENY as escalate-to-human rather than treating APPROVE as sufficient.
Stop calling approve_session() on a smart verdict at approval.py:1275-1276 — make model-granted approval one-shot, matching the deliberate one-shot policy already applied to execute_code approvals.

findings.summary: Logs are durable and redacted but free-form, with no structured event schema for tool invocations or approval decisions.
findings.description: The remit requires tool invocations, approval decisions and session lifecycle events to be recorded to durable structured logs sufficient to reconstruct what the agent did. The infrastructure is durable, rotated, redacted and session-tagged, but every record is a formatted message string, so reconstructing which tool ran with which arguments and whether an approval was granted means regex-mining prose rather than querying fields. No desktop.log was found in the desktop source at all — the only desktop log writer is the updater.
policy_rule_text: Tool invocations, approval decisions, and session lifecycle events MUST be recorded to durable, structured logs (`agent.log` / `gateway.log`; `desktop.log` for the desktop layer) sufficient to reconstruct what the agent did.

evidence.snippet: _LOG_FORMAT at :45 is "%(asctime)s %(levelname)s%(session_tag)s %(name)s: %(message)s" — a prose message field with no tool name, arguments, decision or outcome as discrete keys, applied to all three handlers at :215-243
the approval decision that most needs an audit record is emitted as a free-text logger.warning with the command truncated to 200 characters, not as a structured approval event

recommended_actions: Add a JSON-lines action log beside the existing handlers in hermes_logging.py carrying discrete fields — timestamp, session id, tool name, arguments digest, approval decision, outcome — so tool use and approvals are queryable by detection rules.

Emit the approval outcome in tools/approval.py through that structured channel at every branch (hardline block, auto-approve, smart verdict, operator choice) rather than only as a warning on the auto-approve path.

findings.summary: Desktop dependencies are caret-ranged and the auto-update feed points at a personal GitHub account rather than the vendor org.
findings.description: The agent root pins every direct dependency exactly and documents why; the desktop half of the same subject ships caret ranges throughout, including posthog-js and electron-updater. A committed lockfile keeps installs reproducible, which caps this at Medium, but a fresh resolve or a lockfile refresh silently widens the intake. Separately, the update channel that autoInstallOnAppQuit consumes resolves to a personal account while the application identity is the vendor's.

evidence.snippet: dependencies block lines 28-40 — every entry caret-ranged including "posthog-js" and "electron-updater"; package-lock.json is committed, so today's installs are reproducible but the declared intake is not pinned

publish block resolves owner "fathah" repo "hermes-desktop" while appId is com.nousresearch.hermes and vendor is "Nous Research"; dev-app-update.yml repeats it and index.ts:1623 sets autoInstallOnAppQuit = true

recommended_actions: Pin the desktop runtime dependencies exactly in package.json, matching the discipline already documented in the agent's pyproject.toml, starting with electron, electron-updater and posthog-js.

Move the publish target in electron-builder.yml and dev-app-update.yml to the vendor organisation that owns the application identity, so the auto-update channel and the code-signing identity share a trust root.

findings.summary: The main config file accepts a plaintext sudo password, against the remit's rule that credentials live in the operator credential file.
findings.description: The remit states credentials must not be written into the main config file and belong in the operator credential file with tight permissions. terminal.sudo_password is a documented config.yaml key that the runtime reads, and config.yaml does not receive the 0600 treatment the credential file gets. The shipped example is commented out and carries an explicit plaintext warning, and the credential is a local sudo password rather than a provider key, so the exposure is narrow.
policy_rule_text: Credentials MUST NOT be written into the main config file or into version control; they belong in the operator credential file with tight permissions (or a dedicated secret store).

evidence.snippet: "# sudo_password: \"hunter2\"  # Optional: pipe a sudo password via sudo -S. SECURITY WARNING: plaintext." inside the terminal block at :167-174, documenting the credential slot in the main config file

os.chmod(path, 0o600) is applied to the credential file only; the comment at :571 notes 0600 on the shared config path would break multi-process gateway setups, so config.yaml keeps looser permissions

recommended_actions: Move terminal.sudo_password resolution to the operator credential file or the existing SUDO_PASSWORD environment path only, and have config loading reject the key in config.yaml with a message pointing at the credential file.
Remove the commented example from cli-config.yaml.example:173 so the main config file is not documented as a credential location.

positives.title: Unconditional hardline command floor, evaluated before every bypass
positives.description: HARDLINE_PATTERNS blocks root-filesystem deletion, mkfs, raw block-device writes, fork bombs, kill -1 and shutdown/reboot, and is checked before yolo mode, approvals.mode=off and cron approve-mode, so no session-level setting can pass them through. Yolo state is additionally frozen at module import so an in-process skill cannot enable it at runtime.

positives.title: API server refuses to start without an authentication key
positives.description: The API adapter returns False at startup when API_SERVER_KEY is unset — explicitly including loopback-only binds — and refuses a placeholder-strength key on a network bind, with every route calling _check_auth and comparing the bearer token via hmac.compare_digest.

positives.title: Messaging gateway authorization fails closed
positives.description: _is_user_authorized ends in a default deny — with no allowlist configured it falls through to GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS, which is unset by default, so an unlisted caller is refused rather than admitted.

positives.title: Webhook routes require an HMAC secret and fail closed per request
positives.description: Routes without a secret are rejected at startup and again at request time before any body is processed, and the INSECURE_NO_AUTH test escape hatch is refused when the adapter is not bound to loopback.

positives.title: Python dependencies exact-pinned with a committed lockfile
positives.description: Every direct dependency is pinned to ==X.Y.Z with an in-file rationale citing a real PyPI worm incident, uv.lock is committed, and provider-specific packages are deliberately kept out of the core set and lazy-installed to shrink the supply-chain blast radius.

positives.title: MCP subprocess environment is built from an allowlist
positives.description: _build_safe_env starts from an empty dict and copies only PATH, HOME, USER, LANG, LC_ALL, TERM, SHELL, TMPDIR and XDG_* plus operator-declared vars, so a new credential added anywhere in the process environment is excluded by default rather than requiring a denylist update.

positives.title: Skill-declared credential passthrough cannot override sandbox scrubbing
positives.description: register_env_passthrough refuses to register any variable in the Hermes provider blocklist regardless of whether the request came from a skill's frontmatter or from the operator's config.yaml — the remediation for GHSA-rhgp-j443-p4rf, where a malicious skill declared OPENAI_API_KEY as passthrough to receive it in the execute_code child.

positives.title: Electron renderer hardened and agent output rendered inert
positives.description: The main window and every attached webview run with nodeIntegration: false, contextIsolation: true, sandbox: true and a navigation allowlist, and AgentMarkdown renders model output through react-markdown without rehype-raw and restricts link protocols to http/https/mailto, so agent-produced markup is displayed as data.

positives.title: No committed credentials in either source root
positives.description: A sweep of both trees for OpenAI-style keys, GitHub PATs, Slack tokens, AWS access-key IDs and PEM private-key headers returned zero hits, no .env file is committed, and hermes_cli/config.py chmods the operator credential file to 0600 on creation.

rows.content_type: plaintext rotating log, timestamp + level + session tag + logger name
rows.purpose: INFO+ catch-all for agent, tool and session activity, including the auto-approval warning line
quick-triage stream for errors and warnings, including hardline and sudo-stdin blocks

rows.content_type: plaintext rotating log, records from gateway.* loggers only
rows.purpose: platform adapters, session management, slash commands and delivery events
electron-updater check, download and install events for the desktop self-update path

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Partial. Hermes has genuine, code-level controls in every RAISE category — an unconditional destructive-command floor that runs before every bypass, per-route bearer authentication that refuses to start without a key, default-deny caller authorization, exact-pinned Python dependencies with a committed lockfile, and security regression tests traceable to named advisories — which is well above the norm for a self-hosted personal agent. What holds the score at Partial is that the controls are denylists and heuristics by design, and that the default configuration ships the one combination the project's own security policy calls unsupported: untrusted input surfaces on the host terminal backend. Observability and supply-chain integrity are the weakest legs: logs are durable and redacted but free-form, and the desktop runtime install path has no integrity verification at all.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: The agent is general-purpose by design and the remit authorizes that, but scope is genuinely enforced in code — toolsets.py defines per-surface toolsets (the webhook toolset is deliberately narrowed to web_search/web_extract), tools/mcp_tool.py supports per-server include/exclude tool filters, and tools/delegate_tool.py caps subagent concurrency and spawn depth. No capability was found at runtime outside the remit's Known Good Baseline.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: External content is screened by a single shared pattern library (tools/threat_patterns.py) with three scopes, invisible-unicode detection and filler-word bypass resistance, and agent/prompt_builder.py replaces a matching context file with a placeholder rather than loading it — real controls, but denylists with named holes: MCP tool descriptions are scanned warn-only, ~/.hermes/SOUL.md is agent-writable with no approval gate, and the custom-endpoint provider key is missing from the subprocess strip set.

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: Multiple deterministic gates are operative on the agent's path — HARDLINE_PATTERNS is evaluated before yolo, approvals.mode=off and cron approve-mode, yolo state is frozen at import so an in-process skill cannot set it, api_server.py refuses to start without API_SERVER_KEY and compares it with hmac.compare_digest, and _is_user_authorized defaults to deny. The accepted gap is large and documented: outside CLI/gateway/cron the approval gate returns approved, and the default local terminal backend puts LLM-emitted commands on the host.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: The Python side is exemplary — every direct dependency exact-pinned to ==X.Y.Z with a written anti-supply-chain rationale, uv.lock committed, provider-specific packages lazy-installed to shrink blast radius, and tools/osv_check.py queries OSV for malware advisories before launching an npx/uvx MCP server. That is undercut in the same subject by a desktop install path that pipes a script fetched from a mutable branch into bash with no integrity verification, caret-ranged desktop dependencies, and an update feed pointed at a personal GitHub account.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: Adversarial testing demonstrably changed the design, not just the config — tools/env_passthrough.py now refuses to register Hermes provider credentials because of GHSA-rhgp-j443-p4rf, hermes_cli/web_server.py gained Host-header validation for GHSA-ppp5-vxwm-4cf7, and dedicated regression suites exist on both sides (tests/tools/test_skills_guard.py, test_cron_prompt_injection.py, test_execute_code_approval_cluster.py; desktop electron-security.test.ts, askpass-security.test.ts). No evidence of an ongoing red-team cadence beyond advisory-driven regression work.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: Logging is durable and thoughtfully built — hermes_logging.py installs rotating agent.log/errors.log/gateway.log handlers with a RedactingFormatter and a per-thread session tag for correlation — but the format is a free-form message string with no structured event schema, so tool invocations and approval decisions cannot be parsed into detection rules, and no alerting surface was found.
